title: Execution over resources: Two ways to use the same slide.
author: Adam Robbins
summary: Adam Robbins, reflecting on a whole-school CPD session about checking for listening (CfL), compares two near-identical ways teachers can use the same explanation slide -- one where the teacher explains everything and only then asks a cold-call question with the answer already visible, and one where the teacher asks the CfL question before revealing the corresponding information on the slide. Using a "ratio lens" of participation ratio (how many students are thinking) and think ratio (how hard they're thinking), Robbins argues both versions keep the participation ratio identical since both use cold call, but the think ratio diverges sharply: in the first version, students can simply read the visible answer off the slide, undermining the value of the question and adding a redundancy cost since reading and listening compete for the same working-memory channel. In the second version, students must attend to the spoken explanation because the information isn't yet visible, creating what Robbins calls a "threat of inference" that motivates genuine listening, and the class hears the content twice -- once spoken, once confirmed on the slide -- reinforcing recall. He grounds the redundancy point in cognitive load theory's finding that simultaneously reading and hearing the same words competes for shared working-memory resources rather than reinforcing them. Robbins closes by arguing that resource design gets disproportionate attention because it produces an artifact to evaluate, when how a resource is actually used in the room is often the more consequential variable.
points: Robbins's \"ratio lens\" splits classroom questioning into participation ratio (how many students think) and think ratio (how hard they think), showing two techniques can share the same participation ratio while differing sharply in think ratio.

Version 1 (explain, then question with the answer already visible) risks a redundancy cost: cognitive load theory holds that reading written text and listening to speech compete for the same working-memory channel rather than reinforcing each other.
Version 2 (question before the answer is revealed) creates a \"threat of inference\" that motivates genuine listening, since students cannot simply read the answer off the slide to fake engagement.
Robbins's closing argument -- that resource design gets more attention than resource use because it leaves a visible artifact -- reframes CPD priorities toward technique, not just materials.
quotes: Recently I ran a whole school CPD session about the concept of checking for listening (CfL) as a way of helping students pay attention to key areas.
When we consider the think ratio the two options significantly diverge. In 1 the think ratio is low. The teacher is asking the question at the end and all the information is on the slide.
Cognitive load theory suggests that the fact that reading written words and listening to speech are processed through similar channels of the working memory.
This accountability or ‘threat of inference’ helps motivate them to pay attention.
Resource design is important, but it’s not the only important thing. It’s easy to focus on because it has an artifact that we can evaluate at the end.
